walkthroughs.body_html:
International Trade and the Global Economy — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

International Trade and the Global Economy brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with International Trade and the Global Economy.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Specialisation based on lowest opportunity cost is:
options: Absolute advantage
Comparative advantage
Free trade
Protectionism

mcqs.q: A tariff is a tax on:
options: Exports
Imports
Domestic production
Consumption

mcqs.q: What determines the size of the fiscal multiplier?
options: The fiscal multiplier is always 2 or 3.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Mainly the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) — the higher the share of extra income people spend domestically, the bigger the multiplier. Leakages (saving, imports, taxes) reduce the multiplier.
Revenue is profit before tax and profit is revenue after tax.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between revenue and profit?
options: The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Revenue and profit mean the same thing.
Revenue is total income from sales (price x quantity); profit is what remains after deducting costs from revenue.
Revenue is profit before tax and profit is revenue after tax.
An initial injection of spending circulates as recipients spend portions, generating more income — total effect on GDP is larger than the initial injection.
Revenue is profit before tax and profit is revenue after tax.
The multiplier is the rate at which interest compounds.
The multiplier means government spending is always good because it multiplies wealth.
